common_name: Primavera Witch Hazel (Pale Yellow Winter-Blooming Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Primavera opens some of the palest, most delicate flowers of any witch hazel cultivar, so give it a backdrop that will not wash the color out.

directions: Primavera is a soft-flowered witch hazel selection, opening pale primrose-yellow, ribbon-petaled blossoms in late winter to very early spring, generally a touch later than the deep-yellow Hamamelis cultivars, which stretches out the flowering window in a mixed witch hazel planting. The subtle color reads best against dark evergreens or a brick wall rather than open sky. Fall foliage turns a clean butter-yellow, and the naturally rounded, vase-shaped habit needs only light shaping right after bloom. Give it consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, since the shallow root system does not tolerate prolonged drought or waterlogging.

common_name: Wisley Supreme Witch Hazel (Fragrant Golden Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; site Wisley Supreme close to a path or entry so its strong winter fragrance can be appreciated on cold days.

directions: Selected and popularized through trials at the RHS garden at Wisley, this cultivar produces abundant clusters of golden-yellow, spidery flowers with a notably strong, sweet fragrance that carries well beyond the plant on still winter days. Bloom typically peaks in mid to late winter, filling gaps in the shaded border when little else is showing color. Fall foliage turns warm yellow-gold before dropping to reveal the flower-studded bare branches. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and prune only lightly right after flowering, since witch hazel resents heavy pruning and does not tolerate either drought or soggy ground.

common_name: Heart Throb Kousa Dogwood (Deep Pink-Bracted Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Heart Throb develops its deepest rose-red bract color with a half-day or more of direct sun.

directions: Heart Throb is among the deepest-colored pink Kousa dogwood cultivars, opening rose-red, heart-shaped bracts in late spring that hold their intense color better in heat than many older pink selections, followed by raspberry-textured red fruit that draws songbirds in late summer. Fall foliage turns a rich maroon-purple. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and water deeply through the first two seasons while the root system establishes. Like other Kousa selections it blooms several weeks after native flowering dogwood and shows much better resistance to anthracnose and dogwood borer, making it a dependable choice where native dogwood has struggled with disease.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; National grows more vigorously and uniformly upright than many older seedling-grown Kousa dogwoods.

directions: National is a vigorous, heavy-flowering Kousa dogwood selection prized for its uniform, upright-oval habit and reliably dense coverage of large, pointed white bracts each late spring, followed by abundant raspberry-like red fruit that persists into fall and feeds birds. Fall foliage color runs from red to reddish-purple. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, watering deeply during establishment; its faster growth rate and strong central leader make it a good choice where a more predictable, tree-form specimen is wanted than seed-grown Kousa stock typically provides. Like other Kousa selections it resists the anthracnose and borer problems common to native flowering dogwood.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in acid, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with afternoon shade; Ballet transplants best while young and dislikes root disturbance, so site it as a permanent specimen from the start.

directions: Ballet was selected for an especially showy summer flower display, its white, camellia-like blossoms slightly larger and more gracefully waved at the petal edges than the species, opening over an extended period in midsummer when few other trees are in bloom. Like other Japanese stewartia it carries the full four-season package: orange-red fall foliage and strikingly mottled, exfoliating bark in gray, cinnamon, and cream that provides the best winter interest of any small flowering tree. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade, and keep soil consistently moist, since stewartia resents both drought stress and compacted, poorly drained sites.

common_name: Milk and Honey Stewartia (Exceptional Bark Japanese Stewartia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in acid, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with afternoon shade; site Milk and Honey where its exceptional trunk can be viewed up close year-round, since bark is its standout feature.

directions: Milk and Honey was selected from a Martha's Vineyard arboretum planting specifically for its outstanding exfoliating bark, which peels away in irregular patches of cream, honey-tan, and warm gray to create a puzzle-piece trunk pattern considered among the finest of any Japanese stewartia selection. It still delivers the species' white, camellia-like summer flowers and orange to burgundy fall foliage, but the bark display carries real weight from late fall through winter once foliage drops. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade, and avoid disturbing the root zone once established, since stewartia transplants poorly as a mature specimen.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; China Snow flowers more heavily and at a younger age than typical seed-grown Chinese fringetree.

directions: China Snow is a heavier-blooming Chinese fringetree selection, producing a denser, more uniform blanket of slender white flower clusters each late spring than typical seedling trees, along with glossier, thicker dark-green foliage that resists summer heat stress well. Male-leaning flowering tends to be showiest, though fruit set can still occur, bringing dark blue-black berries that birds favor in late summer. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; it tolerates heavier clay soils better than many flowering trees provided drainage is adequate, and its tidy rounded habit and attractive furrowed bark give it strong winter structure as well.

common_name: Tokyo Tower Fringetree (Narrow Columnar Chinese Fringetree)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; the narrow columnar habit of Tokyo Tower fits tight side yards and street tree strips where a wide-spreading fringetree would not.

directions: Tokyo Tower is a distinctively narrow, upright-columnar sport of Chinese fringetree, retaining the species' frothy clusters of slender white spring flowers and glossy dark-green summer foliage on a tightly fastigiate frame instead of the typical broad, rounded canopy. The compact footprint makes it useful as a vertical accent, narrow street tree, or screening element where standard fringetrees would outgrow the space. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade, and expect slow, steady growth; like the species it is markedly more heat- and drought-tolerant once established than the native white fringetree, and needs little pruning to maintain its narrow form.
